solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A portion of haggis always lacks flavour at first

indicators.note: 'at first' asks for the opening letter of each of the four words before it

parts.note: the leading letters of haggis, always, lacks and flavour

explanation.surface: A food critic complains that a serving of haggis is always bland.
explanation.walkthrough: The first four letters of the surface's words spell the answer, and 'A portion' at the front is the definition, not part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A half is one of two equal shares of something, so it is a portion of the whole.

clue.text: Trousers for fashionable types

definitions.meaning: trousers cut to sit on the hips rather than the waist
people who follow the latest trends in culture and style

explanation.walkthrough: In British English, hipsters are also low-slung trousers (Americans say hip-huggers), which is the sense a non-British solver may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses share one word: low-waisted slacks, and trendy people with self-consciously cool taste.

clue.text: Place is somewhat foul, i.e. unpleasant

indicators.note: 'somewhat' means only partly, so just a stretch of the following words is taken

parts.note: runs from the end of foul, through i.e., into the start of unpleasant

explanation.surface: A visitor describes a grim spot as rather nasty and disagreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'i.e.' looks like a writer's aside but supplies the middle two letters of the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieu is French for place, used in English mainly in the phrase 'in lieu of', meaning in place of.

clue.text: Yell about terrible tune for quite a long time

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the yell wraps itself around the mangled tune

parts.note: to yell is to cry out

indicators.note: a terrible tune is one mangled out of shape, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at an awful song that has been playing for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible tune' looks like a complaint about music, but it is an instruction to rearrange the four letters of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A hundred years is certainly a lengthy period, so the understatement 'quite a long time' fits.

clue.text: Caught person throwing part of game

indicators.note: to catch a remark is to hear it, so what follows is taken by ear

parts.note: one who chucks, or throws, something

explanation.surface: A fielder snaps up a catch from someone lobbing the ball during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' wants to be C, the cricket abbreviation, but here it means heard. In a British accent the final R of the thrower's name is silent, so the two words sound alike. A chukka is one of the timed periods in polo.
explanation.definitionFit: Polo matches are divided into chukkas of about seven minutes each, so one is a section of the game.

clue.text: Celeb ditching the practice of mentioning famous connections

definitions.text: the practice of mentioning famous connections

parts.note: a celebrity is a big name
to ditch something is to drop it

explanation.surface: A star gives up the habit of boasting about which famous people they know.
explanation.walkthrough: Each of the first two words translates straight into one half of the hyphenated answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Name-dropping means casually citing well-known acquaintances to impress others, exactly the habit the definition describes.

clue.text: Inconvenient direction hospital worker may once have gone?

parts.note: an old word meaning 'to' or 'towards', which is why the clue says 'once'
a room or section of a hospital where patients stay
surface padding that frames the scene; 'once' flags the old-fashioned word for direction

explanation.surface: A playful question about where a nurse might have been sent in bygone days.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a little scene: in old-fashioned language a hospital worker would go 'unto ward'. The question mark flags this whimsical reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Untoward describes something unexpected and unwelcome, which is close to troublesome or awkward in its effect.

clue.text: University awayday's ending with beer!

indicators.note: the ending of awayday's is its final letter alone

parts.note: last letter of awayday
ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Students on a day trip finish off with a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: An awayday is a British term for a day out, originally a cheap return rail ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is an Ivy League institution in New Haven, Connecticut, an example of the category named.

clue.text: Elaborate item printers get wrong

indicators.note: to elaborate is to work something up into a new form, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: A fancy piece of print work gets botched at the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elaborate' reads as an adjective describing the item, but it is a verb telling you to rework the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To misinterpret is to understand or read something incorrectly, a straightforward synonym pair.

clue.text: Somehow computerise nearly all valuable material

indicators.note: 'nearly all' is the word stopped just short of its end
'somehow' says the letters get there by some unstated arrangement

parts.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
the word minus its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone plans to digitise almost every precious document in an archive.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is COMPUTERISE plus AL, thirteen letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold, silver and platinum are prized, costly substances, so the phrase is a fair description.

clue.text: Sort of info lawyers know to begin with

indicators.note: 'to begin with' takes what each of the three words starts with

parts.note: opening letters of info, lawyers and know

explanation.surface: The kind of facts that attorneys understand from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' reads as a hedge, but 'Sort' alone is the definition and 'of' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilk means kind or type, as in 'people of that ilk'.

clue.text: Urge, say, almost vanished

indicators.note: 'almost vanished' is the synonym cut off before its final letter

parts.note: e.g., for example
vanished is gone, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A craving that, for instance, has nearly disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Urge' reads as a noun in the surface but the definition is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg on is to encourage or push someone to act, a phrasal verb meaning the same as the imperative prompt.

clue.text: I'd forget about trash

indicators.note: 'about' means turned around every which way, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.surface: Someone admits they would not remember the rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trash' looks like a noun but is the verb, to throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: To trash something in the sense of binning it is to dispose of it, so the phrasal verb matches.

clue.text: Look, food is likely a big element of holiday expenditure

definitions.text: likely a big element of holiday expenditure

parts.note: an air is a look or manner, as in 'an air of confidence'
fare is food, as in 'simple fare'

explanation.surface: A traveller notes that meals are probably a large part of trip spending.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests food is the big holiday cost; in fact 'Look' and 'food' are the wordplay and the flight ticket is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The ticket price for a flight is often the largest single cost of a trip abroad.

clue.text: Vision certainly embodied by rowing crew

indicators.note: to be embodied by is to sit inside another body, so 'certainly' goes within the crew

parts.note: a rowing boat with eight oarsmen, and by extension its crew
an emphatic agreement

explanation.surface: A dream of success is shared by all the members of a boat team.
explanation.walkthrough: An eight is the standard name for a racing boat and its crew of eight rowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Vision in its literal sense is the ability to see, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: I told you, the cuts hurt

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go inside it, so 'hurt' is split around 'the'

parts.note: sore means painful or hurt
used as printed

explanation.surface: Someone smugly reminds a friend that they warned them the injuries would sting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cuts' reads as wounds, but 'the' is fodder and 'cuts' is the instruction to insert it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are triumphant retorts said after being proved correct in an argument.

clue.text: Joyful story upset newspaper boss

indicators.note: in a down clue, to upset is to tip over, so the story is turned bottom to top

parts.note: a tale is a story
abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A happy news item annoys the paper's editor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as annoyed in the surface, but it tips the story over.
explanation.definitionFit: Elated means in high spirits, a close synonym of happy and glad.

clue.text: Poet periodically welcomes in a doctor and priest

indicators.note: to welcome someone in is to take them inside, so the poet's letters surround the rest
'periodically' takes letters at regular intervals, here every other one of the poet

parts.note: first and third letters of poet
used as printed
standard abbreviation for doctor

explanation.surface: A writer of verse sometimes has a physician and a clergyman as guests.
explanation.walkthrough: Padre is a common term for a chaplain, especially in the armed forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Padre is Spanish and Italian for father, and in English means a chaplain or clergyman.

clue.text: Cheek, or something next to it!

definitions.meaning: the part of the face beside the cheek

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is cheek meaning impudence; the second reads cheek as the body part, and the lip lies beside it. The exclamation mark marks the playful switch.
explanation.definitionFit: Lip is slang for insolent talk, and also the fleshy edge of the mouth adjoining the face's side.

clue.text: Engine noise is mostly clean, right?

indicators.note: 'mostly' keeps most of the word, dropping its last letter

parts.note: clean is pure, minus its final letter
standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A mechanic asks whether a motor's sound is largely smooth.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'right?' is a question tag, but it is just the single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-tuned motor running smoothly makes a low, steady hum like a contented cat.

clue.text: Large amount of money in substantial property

definitions.meaning: informal for a fortune, as when someone makes a killing on the stock market
a large imposing building, such as a stately home

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as wealth tied up in real estate, but 'in' is only a link between two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a fortune is a pile, and a grand old mansion is also called a pile.

clue.text: Getting redundant sign updated

indicators.note: an updated sign has been redone, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: An obsolete notice is being replaced with a new version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' reads as receiving, but here it means grasping, as in 'I'm not getting the joke'.
explanation.definitionFit: To get something informally is to comprehend it, so the present participles match.

clue.text: Discredited official silenced after losing millions

indicators.note: 'after' puts the silenced word second, behind the official

parts.note: short for referee, the match official

indicators.note: 'losing millions' removes the abbreviation for millions from the word

parts.note: silenced is muted
standard abbreviation for millions, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A disgraced bureaucrat is gagged after a costly financial loss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Official' sounds like a civil servant but is the sports referee.
explanation.definitionFit: A claim that has been refuted has been proved false, which is to say shown up as untrue.

clue.text: Dog possibly swallows small bug

indicators.note: to swallow is to take inside, so the dog holds 'small'

parts.note: a dog is one example of a pet, hence 'possibly'
standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A hound eats a tiny insect.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog eating a bug is a natural picture; the bug is the definition, not the thing swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A pest is an insect or creature that damages crops or homes, as a bug can be.
